title: Your Gut Has a 'Second Brain' — Here's What Science Now Knows
excerpt: On World Brain Day 2026, emerging research reveals how the 500 million neurons lining your gut communicate with your brain, influencing mood, appetite, and diseases from Parkinson's to long COVID.
body:
• The enteric nervous system (ENS) in the gut contains over 500 million neurons, functioning as a 'second brain.'
  • Research suggests that many neurological conditions may have origins in the gut rather than just the brain.
  • Approximately 95% of the body's serotonin, linked to mood regulation, is produced in the gut.
  • The vagus nerve facilitates communication between the gut and brain, with 90% of signals traveling from the gut to the brain.

Your gut has its own nervous system — a sprawling mesh of over 500 million neurons running the length of your digestive tract, from esophagus to colon. Scientists call it the enteric nervous system (ENS). Informally, it's your "second brain."

On World Brain Day, observed annually on July 22 and marked this year under the theme "Brain Health: Access for All," the gut-brain connection has drawn fresh attention from neurologists worldwide. The World Federation of Neurology, which spearheads the day, estimates that over 3.4 billion people globally live with neurological conditions — many of which, researchers now believe, may have roots not just in the skull, but in the abdomen.

What Is the Enteric Nervous System?

The ENS contains roughly the same number of neurons as a cat's brain, according to Brian Gulbransen, a neuroscience professor at Michigan State University. Unlike other peripheral nerves that simply relay messages between the brain and body, the ENS operates with a degree of autonomy.

"It's like this second brain in our gut. It's an extensive network of neurons and glia that line our intestines."

— Brian Gulbransen, MSU Foundation Professor, Michigan State University

Stanford neurosurgeon Julia Kaltschmidt has shown that if a mouse gut is removed and kept alive in fluid, it continues to contract and push contents forward on its own — no brain required. The ENS uses over 30 different neurotransmitters, many identical to those found in the brain, including serotonin. Roughly 95% of the body's serotonin — a chemical closely tied to mood regulation — is produced in the gut, not in the brain.

The Vagus Nerve Highway

The gut and brain maintain constant dialogue through the vagus nerve, a major neural highway connecting the two systems. About 90% of the signals traveling through the vagus nerve run from the gut upward to the brain, not the other way around, according to research cited in Scientific American.

This two-way communication — known as the gut-brain axis — allows gut microbes to influence mood, sleep, appetite, and cognitive function. A 2022 Stanford study found that mice with certain gut bacterial profiles were more motivated to exercise; when researchers swapped the microbiomes via fecal transplant, exercise enthusiasm switched along with it. The bacteria produced fatty acid metabolites that triggered dopamine release in the brain.

New Discoveries: Neuropods and the 'Neurobiotic Sense'

A breakthrough study published in Nature by Duke University neuroscientists Diego Bohórquez and M. Maya Kaelberer identified a previously unknown sensory system in the gut called the "neurobiotic sense." Tiny sensor cells called neuropods, lining the colon's surface, detect proteins released by gut bacteria and fire rapid signals to the brain through the vagus nerve to regulate appetite.

"Looking ahead, I think this work will be especially helpful for the broader scientific community to explain how our behavior is influenced by microbes."

— Diego Bohórquez, Professor of Medicine and Neurobiology, Duke University

In experiments, fasted mice given a dose of the bacterial protein flagellin directly in the colon ate less. Mice engineered without the receptor for flagellin showed no such restraint — they kept eating and gained weight. The findings suggest the gut sends a direct "we've had enough" signal to the brain.

Implications for Parkinson's and Long COVID

The gut-brain axis has drawn particular interest in Parkinson's disease research. Gut symptoms like constipation and heartburn often precede movement symptoms by years or decades. A 2024 study by Harvard researchers found that damage to the upper digestive tract increases Parkinson's risk significantly. Misfolded alpha-synuclein proteins — the hallmark of Parkinson's — can travel from the gut to the brain via the vagus nerve, according to published research. People who have had their vagus nerve severed show a lower risk of developing the disease.

Stanford researchers Christoph Thaiss and Maayan Levy have also linked long COVID's cognitive symptoms — brain fog, memory lapses — to impaired gut-brain signaling. Their 2023 study found that long COVID reduced serotonin levels and vagus nerve activity. When mice modeling the condition were treated with fluoxetine (Prozac), their cognitive function recovered.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

India has long recognized the gut's centrality to health through Ayurvedic traditions that emphasize digestive fire (agni) and gut balance. Modern science is now validating this emphasis with molecular precision. For the diaspora, the research carries practical relevance: dietary shifts that accompany immigration — less fermented food, more processed meals — can alter gut microbiome composition. A Stanford study showed that diets high in fermented foods increased microbiome diversity and lowered inflammation markers. Traditional Indian fermented foods like curd, idli, dosa batter, and pickles may offer protective benefits worth preserving.

Researchers from Indian institutions including Graphic Era Hill University in Dehradun and Swami Rama Himalayan University have published peer-reviewed work in 2026 on the gut-brain axis's role in neurological disease, contributing to a growing body of evidence from the subcontinent.

What's Next

Kaltschmidt's team at Stanford is working toward what she calls a "pacemaker for the gut" — a device that could electrically stimulate enteric neurons to alleviate chronic constipation linked to aging and neurodegenerative disease. Gulbransen's lab at MSU has received a five-year NIH grant to study how glial cells — the ENS's supporting cast — modulate gut neural circuits, with potential implications for treating IBS and inflammatory bowel disease, conditions affecting 10-15% of Americans.

As Kaltschmidt puts it: "This system not only keeps the gut working, but plays a central role in health and disease and perhaps even in our experience of the mind."
nri_angle: Traditional Indian fermented foods like curd, idli, and pickles may support gut microbiome diversity — a protective factor validated by modern science as dietary shifts during immigration alter gut health.
